foundations.title: Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand
foundations.action: Confirm registration, practising status, competence and the authority required for the task.
foundations.record: Discuss the person’s goals, language, cultural supports and preferred whānau involvement. Use supervision to test the effect of bias, colonisation, poverty and institutional barriers on the formulation. Connect CPD to feedback and the current SWRB requirements rather than assuming that attending a course proves competence. Explain the service complaint route and when a professional concern belongs with SWRB. Health and disability service concerns may also engage the Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC). Identify the actual issue and remedy rather than sending every concern to the same body.

care-support.title: Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand
care-support.action: Identify the responsible funder and referral route, including NASC or another applicable service.
care-support.record: Describe the person’s goals, daily support needs, environmental barriers and existing support. Check the evidence needed for eligibility and explain the decision and funding allocation separately. Confirm the provider, start date, whānau willingness and contingency for gaps or changing needs. Ask the relevant assessment or funding body for reasons and the applicable reassessment, review or complaint route. DSS publishes current assessment information. Track disputes with different funders separately and do not describe a referral to another agency as a resolved need.

mca.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand
mca.action: Specify the treatment or other decision and provide the support needed for participation.
mca.record: Identify the applicable consent or PPPR framework and record decision-specific evidence. Verify the scope and operation of any enduring power of attorney or court order. If relying on Right 7(4), check its conditions, efforts to ascertain the person’s views and consultation requirements. HDC and the independent advocacy service provide routes concerning consumer rights. PPPR court orders and representative disputes may require Family Court or other legal advice. The appropriate review depends on whether the issue is a service breach, capacity decision or representative’s authority.

dols.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand
dols.action: Describe actual restrictions and the person’s wishes, including what happens when they want to leave.
dols.record: Identify the applicable service standard and separate consent, representative authority and any compulsory-care power. Obtain specialist advice about the scope of the order or legal basis where confinement is proposed. Document alternatives, authorisation, monitoring, independent support and a plan to reduce restrictions. Consumer-rights complaints and advocacy are available through the HDC framework. Where a person is under the compulsory mental-health or intellectual-disability Acts, district inspectors have specific rights-protection functions. Identify the applicable court or tribunal review rather than assuming a single liberty procedure.

mha.title: Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand
mha.action: Check whether the operative 1992 route or a subsequently commenced provision applies.
mha.record: Assess the actual mental-disorder and risk or self-care evidence against the relevant statutory criteria. Identify the required clinical assessment, notices, review stage and the person’s cultural and whānau support. Separate compulsory psychiatric treatment from unrelated healthcare consent and discharge-support decisions. District inspectors are independent lawyers who explain rights, investigate concerns and help with access to review. Judicial or Mental Health Review Tribunal processes depend on legal status. Explain the person’s current rights using the Ministry’s accessible materials and arrange legal support where needed.

safeguarding.title: Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand
safeguarding.action: Identify immediate danger, the adult’s wishes and a safe way to communicate.
safeguarding.record: Choose the relevant police, provider, funder or health/disability complaint route for the facts and setting. Check any specific legal duty and act promptly where its conditions apply. Arrange practical support and follow-up alongside reporting, including continuity if a carer or worker is removed. HDC complaints and independent advocacy can address health and disability consumer rights. Police and the courts address different issues. Record which body has accepted responsibility and how the adult can raise concerns about the response.

children.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand
children.action: Record the concern and use the appropriate Oranga Tamariki or police route where needed.
children.record: Distinguish the assessment, the basis for believing care or protection is needed and any referral for a family group conference. Prepare the child and whānau to understand the concern and participate, with the appropriate coordinator and supports. Record the agreed plan, responsible parties and review, and escalate when the plan is not meeting the child’s needs. Explain participation, support and any applicable court or complaint route. A plan should preserve the child’s voice and show who accepted each action. The statutory process and a practice model do not remove the need for evidence about actual safety.

rights.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand
rights.action: Identify the consumer right, equality issue or public-function decision affecting the person.
rights.record: Ask about language, cultural safety, whānau involvement and accessible participation. Check the applicable privacy rules for collection, notification, use and disclosure; rule 11 governs health-information disclosure. Explain the relevant HDC, advocacy, privacy or other complaint and review route. A serious-threat exception to health-information confidentiality has conditions, including necessity and the applicable requirements concerning authorisation. Use the current Privacy Commissioner guidance and record the reasoning. A police request is not automatically a direction to release a whole file.

sources.title: Aotearoa New Zealand Source Library

sources.record: Record the exact source and provision used, date accessed and any unresolved question.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?
cards.answer: The Social Workers Registration Act 2003, SWRB Code of Conduct and Core Competence Standards anchor professional practice in Aotearoa New Zealand. Registration and a current practising certificate should be distinguished from an employer’s allocation of duties. Specialist statutory roles have additional requirements.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The competence framework includes practice with Māori and attention to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, culture, relationships and safe professional practice. Ask how the person wants whānau, hapū, iwi or other supporters involved. Cultural safety requires reflection on professional power and the person’s experience, rather than adding a cultural label to an unchanged assessment.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Confirm registration, practising status, competence and the authority required for the task. Discuss the person’s goals, language, cultural supports and preferred whānau involvement. Use supervision to test the effect of bias, colonisation, poverty and institutional barriers on the formulation. Connect CPD to feedback and the current SWRB requirements rather than assuming that attending a course proves competence.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the service complaint route and when a professional concern belongs with SWRB. Health and disability service concerns may also engage the Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC). Identify the actual issue and remedy rather than sending every concern to the same body.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating whānau involvement as either automatically required in every decision or automatically excluded by individual consent.

flashcardDecks.title: Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?
cards.answer: Disability Support Services (DSS), Needs Assessment and Service Coordination (NASC), Enabling Good Lives arrangements, health services and ACC have different eligibility and funding roles. Identify the scheme relevant to the person’s circumstances; injury-related support, disability support and older-person services should not be treated as one entitlement.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: DSS guidance describes referral to a NASC provider to understand needs and determine eligibility, with relevant supporting evidence. A needs assessment, allocation of funding and a service beginning are separate events. Check the current assessment and funding arrangements rather than relying on an old agency name or contract.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the responsible funder and referral route, including NASC or another applicable service. Describe the person’s goals, daily support needs, environmental barriers and existing support. Check the evidence needed for eligibility and explain the decision and funding allocation separately. Confirm the provider, start date, whānau willingness and contingency for gaps or changing needs.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Ask the relevant assessment or funding body for reasons and the applicable reassessment, review or complaint route. DSS publishes current assessment information. Track disputes with different funders separately and do not describe a referral to another agency as a resolved need.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming that one diagnosis, one assessment or one funding approval covers every service need.

flashcardDecks.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?
cards.answer: Right 7 of the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights addresses informed choice and consent, presumes competence and preserves choice to the extent of a person’s competence. The Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988 (PPPR) provides routes including welfare guardianship, property orders and enduring powers of attorney.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Where a consumer is not competent and no legally entitled representative is available, Right 7(4) has a specific framework. It is not a general rule that any relative may sign. Read the provision and the particular appointment before identifying who may act and what decision standard applies.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Specify the treatment or other decision and provide the support needed for participation. Identify the applicable consent or PPPR framework and record decision-specific evidence. Verify the scope and operation of any enduring power of attorney or court order. If relying on Right 7(4), check its conditions, efforts to ascertain the person’s views and consultation requirements.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: HDC and the independent advocacy service provide routes concerning consumer rights. PPPR court orders and representative disputes may require Family Court or other legal advice. The appropriate review depends on whether the issue is a service breach, capacity decision or representative’s authority.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating diminished competence as loss of every choice or assuming financial authority includes healthcare.

flashcardDecks.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?
cards.answer: Restrictions may engage the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, the consumer Code, PPPR arrangements and, in specific circumstances, compulsory mental-health or intellectual-disability legislation. A welfare guardian or service plan is not an explanation for every measure used by staff.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Identify whether the measure is an ordinary supported-care arrangement, restraint, seclusion or confinement under a specific statutory power. The Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 has a particular statutory scope; intellectual disability alone does not bring every person within it.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Describe actual restrictions and the person’s wishes, including what happens when they want to leave. Identify the applicable service standard and separate consent, representative authority and any compulsory-care power. Obtain specialist advice about the scope of the order or legal basis where confinement is proposed. Document alternatives, authorisation, monitoring, independent support and a plan to reduce restrictions.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Consumer-rights complaints and advocacy are available through the HDC framework. Where a person is under the compulsory mental-health or intellectual-disability Acts, district inspectors have specific rights-protection functions. Identify the applicable court or tribunal review rather than assuming a single liberty procedure.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating a care plan, guardian’s agreement or disability diagnosis as universal authority for confinement.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?
cards.answer: The Ministry of Health states that the Mental Health Act 2026 received Royal Assent on 9 July 2026 and is to commence on 1 July 2028. Until replacement takes effect, the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 remains the operative framework. Preparation for the new system must be distinguished from present powers and rights.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Under the 1992 framework, compulsory assessment and treatment require the statutory mental-disorder criteria and staged procedures. Clinical disagreement, unusual beliefs or a diagnosis alone do not establish all criteria. Use the current Ministry guidelines and authorised clinical roles for the particular stage.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Check whether the operative 1992 route or a subsequently commenced provision applies. Assess the actual mental-disorder and risk or self-care evidence against the relevant statutory criteria. Identify the required clinical assessment, notices, review stage and the person’s cultural and whānau support. Separate compulsory psychiatric treatment from unrelated healthcare consent and discharge-support decisions.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: District inspectors are independent lawyers who explain rights, investigate concerns and help with access to review. Judicial or Mental Health Review Tribunal processes depend on legal status. Explain the person’s current rights using the Ministry’s accessible materials and arrange legal support where needed.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating the 2026 Act as fully operational before its commencement.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?
cards.answer: Adult safety concerns can engage police, health or disability services, provider safeguarding arrangements, the HDC framework and specific criminal-law duties. There is no reason to assume that one overseas adult-protection procedure applies across these settings.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Crimes Act 1961 includes offences concerning ill-treatment or neglect and failure to protect a child or vulnerable adult in defined circumstances. Check the actual duty and the person’s role; do not simplify it into a universal reporting rule for every adult concern. DSS quality and safeguarding arrangements relate to the services within its remit.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify immediate danger, the adult’s wishes and a safe way to communicate. Choose the relevant police, provider, funder or health/disability complaint route for the facts and setting. Check any specific legal duty and act promptly where its conditions apply. Arrange practical support and follow-up alongside reporting, including continuity if a carer or worker is removed.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: HDC complaints and independent advocacy can address health and disability consumer rights. Police and the courts address different issues. Record which body has accepted responsibility and how the adult can raise concerns about the response.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming a provider incident report resolves all legal duties or covers safety outside the provider’s remit.

flashcardDecks.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?
cards.answer: The Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 provides the care-and-protection framework, including reports of concern and family group conferences. Current Oranga Tamariki practice guidance explains assessment, referral, preparation, participation and implementation. A family group conference is a statutory process with defined roles, not simply an informal family meeting.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Establish the child’s safety and views alongside whānau relationships, cultural identity and practical support. Use the current Act and policy for duties and powers; professional commitments to culturally safe practice should not be confused with an assumption that every historical statutory provision remains unchanged.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Record the concern and use the appropriate Oranga Tamariki or police route where needed. Distinguish the assessment, the basis for believing care or protection is needed and any referral for a family group conference. Prepare the child and whānau to understand the concern and participate, with the appropriate coordinator and supports. Record the agreed plan, responsible parties and review, and escalate when the plan is not meeting the child’s needs.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain participation, support and any applicable court or complaint route. A plan should preserve the child’s voice and show who accepted each action. The statutory process and a practice model do not remove the need for evidence about actual safety.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating agreement at a family meeting as proof that a safe, authorised and deliverable plan exists.

flashcardDecks.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?
cards.answer: The Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights, Human Rights Act 1993, New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 and professional standards answer different rights questions. Establish the provider and function involved before choosing the relevant route.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Privacy Act 2020 and Health Information Privacy Code govern information handling in their respective scope. The Privacy Commissioner publishes a version of the Health Information Privacy Code in force from 1 May 2026, reflecting the new indirect-collection requirements. Use that current version rather than an unchanged 2020 download.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the consumer right, equality issue or public-function decision affecting the person. Ask about language, cultural safety, whānau involvement and accessible participation. Check the applicable privacy rules for collection, notification, use and disclosure; rule 11 governs health-information disclosure. Explain the relevant HDC, advocacy, privacy or other complaint and review route.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: A serious-threat exception to health-information confidentiality has conditions, including necessity and the applicable requirements concerning authorisation. Use the current Privacy Commissioner guidance and record the reasoning. A police request is not automatically a direction to release a whole file.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using an outdated privacy-code version or treating collection and disclosure as the same legal decision.

The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.
Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.
Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.
Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.
Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.
The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.
Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.

Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.
Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.
Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.
Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.
A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.
Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.
Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.
An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.
A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.
An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

theoryLenses.title: Ecological Systems Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.
test: What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

theoryLenses.title: Strengths-Based Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.
test: What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

theoryLenses.title: Trauma-Informed Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.
test: What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

theoryLenses.title: Attachment Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.
test: How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

theoryLenses.title: Systems and Family Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.
test: Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

theoryLenses.title: Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.
test: What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

theoryLenses.title: Crisis Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.
test: What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

theoryLenses.title: Life Course Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.
test: What transitions or losses are happening now?
How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

theoryLenses.title: Task-Centred Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.
test: What problem does the person most want to work on first?
What is the smallest useful next step?
Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

hypothesisSignals.label: Self-neglect, hoarding, home conditions, or repeated crisis presentations.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Think about trauma, executive functioning, environment, identity, isolation, loss, and safeguarding thresholds.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person appears to refuse support, miss visits, or disengage.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Avoid jumping straight to non-compliance. Consider trust, trauma, power, communication, and whether the offer fits the person.

hypothesisSignals.label: Family conflict, carer strain, coercion, or unclear roles are present.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Map roles, power, risk, protective factors, and what happens when professionals intervene.

hypothesisSignals.label: Risk has escalated quickly or a crisis is dominating the assessment.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Separate immediate stabilisation from longer-term formulation and legal route decisions.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is a transition: adolescence to adulthood, hospital discharge, bereavement, moving home, or ageing.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Transitions can disrupt identity, support, eligibility, relationships, and coping.

hypothesisSignals.label: Discrimination, poverty, inaccessible services, stigma, or cultural misunderstanding may be relevant.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Test whether systems are creating or worsening the difficulty.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person or carer feels overwhelmed and cannot see a way forward.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Consider crisis, small steps, stabilisation, advocacy, and practical environmental change.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is mistrust of professionals, fear of services, or repeated complaints.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Explore previous experiences, power, communication, consistency, and whether the person has reason to feel unsafe.

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Safety
childPracticeModels.use: Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What are we worried about, what is working well, and what needs to happen for the child to be safe enough?
test: Can worries be written in plain language that the family understands?
What existing safety has been demonstrated, not just promised?
Who is in the family network and what role can they safely take?

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging
childPracticeModels.use: Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What would wellbeing, safety, permanence, connection, and belonging look like from the child's perspective?
test: What does the child say or show about where they feel safe and connected?
What would meaningful stability look like in daily life?
How are family relationships, identity, culture, and belonging being protected?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety may improve when adult needs and risks are addressed alongside direct work with the child and family network.
test: Which adult needs are directly affecting child safety or care?
Is the plan joined up across children's and adults' services?
Are adult-focused interventions linked to measurable child safety outcomes?

childPracticeModels.title: Contextual Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Harm may be located outside the home, in peer, school, community, or online contexts that parents cannot control alone.
test: Where is harm happening: home, school, peer group, community, online, or transport?
Which context needs intervention, not only which child or parent?
Who has power or influence in that context?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Group Conferencing
childPracticeModels.use: Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The wider family network may hold safe, practical solutions that have not yet been fully mapped or invited in.
test: Who does the child identify as family or trusted network?
What information does the family need before private planning?
How will the plan be checked for safety, clarity, and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Systemic Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The concern may be maintained by family patterns, relationship roles, service responses, or repeated cycles.
test: What pattern repeats, and what keeps it going?
How does each person make sense of the problem?
What would change if one part of the system responded differently?

childPracticeModels.title: Motivational Interviewing
childPracticeModels.use: Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The parent or young person may be caught between reasons to change and reasons to keep things as they are.
test: What does the person want to be different?
What are their reasons for change and reasons against change?
Are we arguing for change so hard that the person argues against it?

childPracticeModels.title: Solution-Focused Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Small exceptions or signs of safety may reveal what can be repeated, strengthened, and built into the plan.
test: When is the problem slightly less serious?
What would one point higher on the safety scale look like?
What has the family already done that helped, even briefly?

childPracticeModels.title: PACE and DDP-Informed Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The child may need relational safety through playfulness, acceptance, curiosity, and empathy before they can reflect or change.
test: How does the child's behaviour make sense as communication or protection?
How can adults stay curious without shaming or escalating?
What helps the child experience safety in the relationship?

childPracticeModels.title: Safe and Together
childPracticeModels.use: Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety work should focus on the perpetrator's pattern of behaviour and avoid blaming the non-abusive parent for the abuse.
test: What is the perpetrator's pattern and impact on the child?
What has the protective parent done to promote safety?
Does the plan increase accountability for the person causing harm?

childPracticeModels.title: Graded Care Profile 2
childPracticeModels.use: Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The quality of care may need structured, observable mapping rather than vague descriptions of neglect.
test: Which care domains are strong, inconsistent, or harmful?
What evidence has been observed rather than assumed?
Is change measurable across time and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Restorative Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Progress may come through relationship repair, accountability, and shared planning rather than only professional direction.
test: Who has been affected and what do they need?
What repair or accountability is realistic and safe?
How will the meeting avoid blame and keep the child central?

childModelSignals.label: Child protection concerns, safety planning, or danger statements are needed.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs clear worries, existing safety, safety goals, family network planning, and review.

childModelSignals.label: Neglect, home conditions, missed health needs, or inconsistent care are central.
childModelSignals.detail: The assessment needs observable evidence, care domains, impact on the child, and change over time.

childModelSignals.label: Domestic abuse is affecting the child or family safety.
childModelSignals.detail: The plan needs perpetrator pattern analysis, protective parent strengths, child impact, and safe information sharing.

childModelSignals.label: Exploitation, adolescent risk, peer harm, school risk, or online/community harm is present.
childModelSignals.detail: Risk may sit outside the home and require contextual mapping beyond parent-focused plans.

childModelSignals.label: The child is in care, on the edge of care, returning home, or permanence is uncertain.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs belonging, stability, identity, relationships, family network options, and safe permanence planning.

childModelSignals.label: Trauma, attachment disruption, mistrust, shame, or relational conflict is central.
childModelSignals.detail: The child may need relational safety and adults who can stay curious, calm, boundaried, and empathic.

childModelSignals.label: There may be wider family or trusted network members who could help.
childModelSignals.detail: The network may hold safe options for care, practical support, supervision, or belonging.

childModelSignals.label: A parent or young person feels ambivalent, defensive, stuck, or hard to engage.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs careful engagement, change talk, respect for autonomy, and clarity about non-negotiable safety.

childModelSignals.label: There has been conflict, harm, school exclusion, relationship breakdown, or a need for repair.
childModelSignals.detail: The work may need accountability, safe dialogue, relationship repair, and a shared plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A service describes a Māori client as disengaged after arranging meetings without the support person they requested.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Ask what made the meetings unsafe or unhelpful and agree how participation should work. Review the earlier interpretation and record the person’s goals and chosen supports. Take the effect of professional and institutional power to supervision, with a concrete change to the next contact.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A person with a longstanding disability develops additional support needs after an injury, and two services each suggest the other should pay.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Map the needs and the scope of each scheme, obtain the actual eligibility decisions and coordinate the interface. Record interim support and unresolved funding responsibility. Keep the person’s desired outcomes visible while the agencies resolve the dispute.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A woman can express a clear preference about treatment but needs information presented in short sessions. Her son says he should sign because he manages her bills.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Provide the communication support and assess the relevant decision. Financial help does not establish healthcare authority. Read any appointment and use the applicable consent framework, preserving the woman’s own choices to the extent she can make them.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A residential provider uses a locked room when a resident becomes distressed and says the welfare guardian approved the behaviour plan.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess immediate safety, the purpose and effect of isolation and the person’s experience. Check the guardian’s powers and the specific legal and service requirements for the measure. Explore communication, environmental and staffing changes, and escalate any missing authority or safeguard.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A team wants to apply a future provision of the 2026 Act because it has been included in a training presentation.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Confirm the commencement date and use the operative legislation and forms for the person’s present assessment. Explain current district-inspector and review rights. Record preparation for the new law as service development, not as the authority for today’s intervention.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An adult using funded support reports that a worker withholds meals as punishment but fears losing the service if they complain.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Establish immediate access to food and safe support, hear the adult privately and preserve the relevant facts. Follow the appropriate safeguarding and complaint routes and consider criminal duties or police involvement. Plan continuity so reporting does not leave the person without essential assistance.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A conference agrees that relatives will support a child, but nobody confirms transport, sleeping arrangements or who will supervise overnight.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Translate the broad agreement into a practical plan with named responsibilities and the child’s view. Verify that the arrangements are available and safe. Use the appropriate review or reconvening process if the plan does not meet the needs identified.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A worker receives sensitive health information from a relative and later receives a police request for the entire record.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the current collection-notification requirements and any applicable exception, then assess disclosure separately. Establish the police request’s purpose and legal basis, share only what the applicable rule permits and document the person’s participation or why authorisation could not appropriately be sought.

printableTemplates.title: Professional Foundations
printableTemplates.summary: Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.
printableTemplates.body:
Professional Foundations
Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Social Workers Registration Act 2003, SWRB Code of Conduct and Core Competence Standards anchor professional practice in Aotearoa New Zealand. Registration and a current practising certificate should be distinguished from an employer’s allocation of duties. Specialist statutory roles have additional requirements.

The competence framework includes practice with Māori and attention to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, culture, relationships and safe professional practice. Ask how the person wants whānau, hapū, iwi or other supporters involved. Cultural safety requires reflection on professional power and the person’s experience, rather than adding a cultural label to an unchanged assessment.

Local pathway:
Confirm registration, practising status, competence and the authority required for the task.
Discuss the person’s goals, language, cultural supports and preferred whānau involvement.
Use supervision to test the effect of bias, colonisation, poverty and institutional barriers on the formulation.
Connect CPD to feedback and the current SWRB requirements rather than assuming that attending a course proves competence.

Recording prompts:
1. Your role and the legal or professional framework
Notes:

2. The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
Notes:

3. Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the service complaint route and when a professional concern belongs with SWRB. Health and disability service concerns may also engage the Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC). Identify the actual issue and remedy rather than sending every concern to the same body.

Sources:
https://swrb.govt.nz/practice/core-competence-standards/
https://swrb.govt.nz/practice/code-of-conduct/
https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2003/0017/latest/whole.html

printableTemplates.title: Social Care and Support
printableTemplates.summary: Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.
printableTemplates.body:
Social Care and Support
Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Disability Support Services (DSS), Needs Assessment and Service Coordination (NASC), Enabling Good Lives arrangements, health services and ACC have different eligibility and funding roles. Identify the scheme relevant to the person’s circumstances; injury-related support, disability support and older-person services should not be treated as one entitlement.

DSS guidance describes referral to a NASC provider to understand needs and determine eligibility, with relevant supporting evidence. A needs assessment, allocation of funding and a service beginning are separate events. Check the current assessment and funding arrangements rather than relying on an old agency name or contract.

Local pathway:
Identify the responsible funder and referral route, including NASC or another applicable service.
Describe the person’s goals, daily support needs, environmental barriers and existing support.
Check the evidence needed for eligibility and explain the decision and funding allocation separately.
Confirm the provider, start date, whānau willingness and contingency for gaps or changing needs.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Ask the relevant assessment or funding body for reasons and the applicable reassessment, review or complaint route. DSS publishes current assessment information. Track disputes with different funders separately and do not describe a referral to another agency as a resolved need.

Sources:
https://www.disabilitysupport.govt.nz/disabled-people/assessment-and-funding/needs-assessment-services
https://www.disabilitysupport.govt.nz/disabled-people/assessment-and-funding/how-to-access-support

printableTemplates.title: Decision-Making and Capacity
printableTemplates.summary: Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.
printableTemplates.body:
Decision-Making and Capacity
Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Right 7 of the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights addresses informed choice and consent, presumes competence and preserves choice to the extent of a person’s competence. The Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988 (PPPR) provides routes including welfare guardianship, property orders and enduring powers of attorney.

Where a consumer is not competent and no legally entitled representative is available, Right 7(4) has a specific framework. It is not a general rule that any relative may sign. Read the provision and the particular appointment before identifying who may act and what decision standard applies.

Local pathway:
Specify the treatment or other decision and provide the support needed for participation.
Identify the applicable consent or PPPR framework and record decision-specific evidence.
Verify the scope and operation of any enduring power of attorney or court order.
If relying on Right 7(4), check its conditions, efforts to ascertain the person’s views and consultation requirements.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
HDC and the independent advocacy service provide routes concerning consumer rights. PPPR court orders and representative disputes may require Family Court or other legal advice. The appropriate review depends on whether the issue is a service breach, capacity decision or representative’s authority.

Sources:
https://www.hdc.org.nz/education/online-learning/consent-for-consumers-who-are-not-competent/
https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1988/0004/latest/whole.html

printableTemplates.title: Restrictions and Liberty
printableTemplates.summary: Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.
printableTemplates.body:
Restrictions and Liberty
Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Restrictions may engage the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, the consumer Code, PPPR arrangements and, in specific circumstances, compulsory mental-health or intellectual-disability legislation. A welfare guardian or service plan is not an explanation for every measure used by staff.

Identify whether the measure is an ordinary supported-care arrangement, restraint, seclusion or confinement under a specific statutory power. The Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 has a particular statutory scope; intellectual disability alone does not bring every person within it.

Local pathway:
Describe actual restrictions and the person’s wishes, including what happens when they want to leave.
Identify the applicable service standard and separate consent, representative authority and any compulsory-care power.
Obtain specialist advice about the scope of the order or legal basis where confinement is proposed.
Document alternatives, authorisation, monitoring, independent support and a plan to reduce restrictions.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Consumer-rights complaints and advocacy are available through the HDC framework. Where a person is under the compulsory mental-health or intellectual-disability Acts, district inspectors have specific rights-protection functions. Identify the applicable court or tribunal review rather than assuming a single liberty procedure.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1990/0109/latest/whole.html
https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1988/0004/latest/whole.html
https://www.health.govt.nz/regulation-legislation/mental-health-and-addiction/mental-health-act/mental-health-district-inspectors

printableTemplates.title: Mental Health
printableTemplates.summary: Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.
printableTemplates.body:
Mental Health
Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Ministry of Health states that the Mental Health Act 2026 received Royal Assent on 9 July 2026 and is to commence on 1 July 2028. Until replacement takes effect, the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 remains the operative framework. Preparation for the new system must be distinguished from present powers and rights.

Under the 1992 framework, compulsory assessment and treatment require the statutory mental-disorder criteria and staged procedures. Clinical disagreement, unusual beliefs or a diagnosis alone do not establish all criteria. Use the current Ministry guidelines and authorised clinical roles for the particular stage.

Local pathway:
Check whether the operative 1992 route or a subsequently commenced provision applies.
Assess the actual mental-disorder and risk or self-care evidence against the relevant statutory criteria.
Identify the required clinical assessment, notices, review stage and the person’s cultural and whānau support.
Separate compulsory psychiatric treatment from unrelated healthcare consent and discharge-support decisions.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
District inspectors are independent lawyers who explain rights, investigate concerns and help with access to review. Judicial or Mental Health Review Tribunal processes depend on legal status. Explain the person’s current rights using the Ministry’s accessible materials and arrange legal support where needed.

Sources:
https://www.health.govt.nz/regulation-legislation/mental-health-and-addiction/repealing-and-replacing-the-mental-health-act
https://www.health.govt.nz/publications/guidelines-to-the-mental-health-compulsory-assessment-and-treatment-act-1992
https://www.health.govt.nz/regulation-legislation/mental-health-and-addiction/mental-health-act/your-rights-under-the-mental-health-act

printableTemplates.title: Adult Safeguarding
printableTemplates.summary: Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.
printableTemplates.body:
Adult Safeguarding
Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Adult safety concerns can engage police, health or disability services, provider safeguarding arrangements, the HDC framework and specific criminal-law duties. There is no reason to assume that one overseas adult-protection procedure applies across these settings.

The Crimes Act 1961 includes offences concerning ill-treatment or neglect and failure to protect a child or vulnerable adult in defined circumstances. Check the actual duty and the person’s role; do not simplify it into a universal reporting rule for every adult concern. DSS quality and safeguarding arrangements relate to the services within its remit.

Local pathway:
Identify immediate danger, the adult’s wishes and a safe way to communicate.
Choose the relevant police, provider, funder or health/disability complaint route for the facts and setting.
Check any specific legal duty and act promptly where its conditions apply.
Arrange practical support and follow-up alongside reporting, including continuity if a carer or worker is removed.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
HDC complaints and independent advocacy can address health and disability consumer rights. Police and the courts address different issues. Record which body has accepted responsibility and how the adult can raise concerns about the response.

Sources:
https://www.disabilitysupport.govt.nz/providers/quality-and-safeguarding/we-can-all-contribute-to-quality-and-safeguarding
https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1961/0043/latest/whole.html

printableTemplates.title: Children, Families and Transitions
printableTemplates.summary: Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.
printableTemplates.body:
Children, Families and Transitions
Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 provides the care-and-protection framework, including reports of concern and family group conferences. Current Oranga Tamariki practice guidance explains assessment, referral, preparation, participation and implementation. A family group conference is a statutory process with defined roles, not simply an informal family meeting.

Establish the child’s safety and views alongside whānau relationships, cultural identity and practical support. Use the current Act and policy for duties and powers; professional commitments to culturally safe practice should not be confused with an assumption that every historical statutory provision remains unchanged.

Local pathway:
Record the concern and use the appropriate Oranga Tamariki or police route where needed.
Distinguish the assessment, the basis for believing care or protection is needed and any referral for a family group conference.
Prepare the child and whānau to understand the concern and participate, with the appropriate coordinator and supports.
Record the agreed plan, responsible parties and review, and escalate when the plan is not meeting the child’s needs.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain participation, support and any applicable court or complaint route. A plan should preserve the child’s voice and show who accepted each action. The statutory process and a practice model do not remove the need for evidence about actual safety.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1989/0024/latest/whole.html
https://practice.orangatamariki.govt.nz/policy/family-group-conferences-for-care-andor-protection-concerns

printableTemplates.title: Rights, Culture and Recording
printableTemplates.summary: Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.
printableTemplates.body:
Rights, Culture and Recording
Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights, Human Rights Act 1993, New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 and professional standards answer different rights questions. Establish the provider and function involved before choosing the relevant route.

The Privacy Act 2020 and Health Information Privacy Code govern information handling in their respective scope. The Privacy Commissioner publishes a version of the Health Information Privacy Code in force from 1 May 2026, reflecting the new indirect-collection requirements. Use that current version rather than an unchanged 2020 download.

Local pathway:
Identify the consumer right, equality issue or public-function decision affecting the person.
Ask about language, cultural safety, whānau involvement and accessible participation.
Check the applicable privacy rules for collection, notification, use and disclosure; rule 11 governs health-information disclosure.
Explain the relevant HDC, advocacy, privacy or other complaint and review route.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
Notes:

2. Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
Notes:

3. Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
Notes:

4. Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
Notes:

5. Access, correction, complaints and review route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
A serious-threat exception to health-information confidentiality has conditions, including necessity and the applicable requirements concerning authorisation. Use the current Privacy Commissioner guidance and record the reasoning. A police request is not automatically a direction to release a whole file.

Sources:
https://www.privacy.org.nz/privacy-principles/codes-of-practice/hipc2020/
https://www.privacy.org.nz/privacy-principles/codes-of-practice/hipc2020/hipc-factsheet-3/
https://www.privacy.org.nz/responsibilities/releasing-personal-information-to-police-and-law-enforcement-agencies/

studentPathwaySteps.task: Confirm registration, practising status, competence and the authority required for the task. Work through the fictional case and explain: Treating whānau involvement as either automatically required in every decision or automatically excluded by individual consent.

studentPathwaySteps.title: Social Care and Support
studentPathwaySteps.task: Identify the responsible funder and referral route, including NASC or another applicable service. Work through the fictional case and explain: Assuming that one diagnosis, one assessment or one funding approval covers every service need.

studentPathwaySteps.title: Decision-Making and Capacity
studentPathwaySteps.task: Specify the treatment or other decision and provide the support needed for participation. Work through the fictional case and explain: Treating diminished competence as loss of every choice or assuming financial authority includes healthcare.

studentPathwaySteps.title: Restrictions and Liberty
studentPathwaySteps.task: Describe actual restrictions and the person’s wishes, including what happens when they want to leave. Work through the fictional case and explain: Treating a care plan, guardian’s agreement or disability diagnosis as universal authority for confinement.

studentPathwaySteps.title: Mental Health
studentPathwaySteps.task: Check whether the operative 1992 route or a subsequently commenced provision applies. Work through the fictional case and explain: Treating the 2026 Act as fully operational before its commencement.

studentPathwaySteps.title: Adult Safeguarding
studentPathwaySteps.task: Identify immediate danger, the adult’s wishes and a safe way to communicate. Work through the fictional case and explain: Assuming a provider incident report resolves all legal duties or covers safety outside the provider’s remit.

studentPathwaySteps.title: Children, Families and Transitions
studentPathwaySteps.task: Record the concern and use the appropriate Oranga Tamariki or police route where needed. Work through the fictional case and explain: Treating agreement at a family meeting as proof that a safe, authorised and deliverable plan exists.

studentPathwaySteps.title: Rights, Culture and Recording
studentPathwaySteps.task: Identify the consumer right, equality issue or public-function decision affecting the person. Work through the fictional case and explain: Using an outdated privacy-code version or treating collection and disclosure as the same legal decision.
